coverage_note: Generated from speaker turns in conversations 1-50 that Jev scored at or above 2.5 for codeable, substantive content (2,987 turns).

rubric: Not codeable: logistics, the consent script, facilitator instructions, or back-channel replies like 'mm-hm'
Minimal: agreeing or reacting with nothing new, or a fragment
Some content: states a fact or opinion without reasons or experience
Substantive: an opinion with reasons, or a concrete experience
Rich: a personal story, an explanation of values, or reasoning that could support several codes

codes.name: Strengthening Community
codes.definition: People describe the relationships, shared practices, and collective spirit that make a place feel connected and able to work together.

children.name: Community Solidarity
children.definition: People emphasize standing together, supporting one another, or acting as a unified community in ordinary times.

evidence.text: I think also just to further add on what Chloe and everyone else said, I think, like, as we begin to look back at the past 250 years and looking at how the OKC bombing fits within that, I think it's important to recognize, like, as Chloe said, like, the community we built, which we founded our nation upon and that same community, how it carried throughout to, like, to the bombing and the recovery and response which we took after that, and how we began to rebuild our city and our state. But what I also think is important is as we move on from here, to not only think about the present but also the future and how we can take these same principles and values as we begin to go. And about, oh, I don't know, seven, eight years ago, Bartlesville finally had a Pride event. And it was in Johnstone Park. I remember my mom and I were there. Like, that made me proud of my community, that there was a group of people, they were just celebrating. Well, fast forward a few years, and in my opinion, what happened was that the group, The Pride event, was happening without incident. It was well attended. The people that didn't want to go, didn't go. The people that wanted to go, went. It was nice. One year, the group decided to advertise the event and put a drag queen on the poster. I won't go into all the details, but there was a very strong contingent of there should be no drag queens performing. And then there was a contingent of, everyone has the right to free speech. And that kind of thing. And it was a lightning rod. Our community was very, very much divided and still on that issue. In some respects, it kind of faded away, and they all kind of went back to their corners. I will. Yeah, it goes up and down, for sure. I will say this, though, and this was one. A part of the lightning rod. There's a television documentary series on hbo, and they came to town to sort of highlight that divisiveness. And it's a. It's a show. I won't name it, but it's a show that. That talks about drag queens and being queer in America and the challenges and joys that come with that. And I happen to be on it. Someone came and talked to me, and here's what was beautiful about it. It was all challenging. It was all very hard, a lot of divisiveness. But there was a gentleman that grew up here. He no longer lives here. He happens to be gay. He saw that. He saw that and he saw me. And basically, my message was, I'm the tourism director. I want to be welcoming to everyone. I don't want anyone to feel unwelcome. And his message to me was, growing up in Bartlesville, I wish I had known someone like you so that it wasn't so hard. And so if there's any sort of silver lining to how challenging that was, it was that it breached sort of some of those struggles or past traumas that people that had here, that chat, you know, that were challenged by just being gay, knowing that there are people in this community that even if they don't agree with who you are or who you love or whatever, they will love you and they will support you because you are a human being. And to me, that is kind of the heart of Bartlesville. That's what I know is even if someone doesn't agree with me, there's been plenty of times I haven't agreed with Earl on some things. There's plenty of times I haven't agreed with Rosie on things. We still can be civil. We can talk, we can have a discussion. We can love and respect them for who they are. And so, to me, despite the challenges of that whole issue that continue, it was nice to know that there were some positives that came out of it, too. That's the. I would say that was not. I don't feel uncomfortable discussing it with this group of people, but it certainly could have been an elephant in the room. It was challenging.

evidence.text: In Ludlow, we have had three, three elementary schools for a population of 21,000. We have the section that I live in which is higher. Middle class houses are between today's price 350 to 500,000. We're all at one elementary school. The next elementary school, which is about four miles away or four street miles away, is the higher end. They're the ones with 500 to a million plus houses. Both mine and that one do not have rentals. We do not have second two family houses. We do not have apartment blocks or single standing houses with a minimum of an acre lot. The other end of town, East street street has the rentals and the two families and the three families and generally low income. When the kids, all the different schools go to school at one point in time, they were getting different educations. My school, where my kids went was got an education that taught them the basics of what they needed to get through in life and to go on to, you know, blue collar workers jobs. The rich school where the kids came from money. They were, they were white collars, they were going to be white collars, they were going to be lawyers, the doctors and the prestigious people from there. The east street kids were the trade kids. So that's important to know because when it came to the Massachusetts Glass aptitude test that the MCAs that they had to take and pass, the east street kids were failing dramatically to the point that the school was about to be teaching taken over by the state for failure to make the grades. The school did, the town did something desperate and they finally realized exactly what was going on in the education system and they switched it so that every kid who's kindergarten and second grade in town will go to one school. All the kids, you know, third, fifth would go to the next school. And sixth and seventh, instead of jumping to the junior high would go to or the middle school would go to the other school. And lo and behold, the test grades went up because they were no longer putting a label on the kids that you're rich or you're medium or you're poor. So it really did in many ways help the kids with their education. That again gave everyone a fair footing for their education. However, school times are staggered. They're staggered. Elementary kids Go earlier, they stay later than the high school and middle kids so that the older kids can be home with the younger kids. What they did was at 7 o' clock now the bus came by your house and all the kids got on the bus. So the kids. And then in the afternoon the kids would do the same thing. So that elementary school day got longer and so did the high school and the middle school. But it also meant that the kids could be on a bus for over an hour and a half traveling to or coming home from school. And the school is less. Any of the schools are less than a 15 minute drive from your house. That was a downfall.
